intro: The OBR has certified the forecast and the Budget is out. Here is how it reads on the afternoon, and how it reads the morning after.

reading.label: Headroom against the stability rule

bands.headline: You have missed your own stability rule.
bands.detail: The rule requires the current budget to be in surplus in the target year. Yours is not. A Chancellor who misses this rule at the Budget has to say at the despatch box how it will be met, or change the rule.

bands.headline: You meet the rule, but by less than your predecessor did.
bands.detail: The March forecast left £23.6bn of headroom. Anything below that invites the question of what happens at the next forecast, because the OBR revises its judgements twice a year and the rule is only tested once.

bands.headline: You meet the rule with roughly the room your predecessor had.
bands.detail: Headroom in this range is normal by recent standards: the March forecast left £23.6bn. It is still small next to the forecast error, which is the point of the second signal below.

bands.headline: You have given yourself unusually large headroom.
bands.detail: More room than any recent Budget has left. It buys insurance against a bad forecast, and it means either taxes are higher or spending lower than they needed to be to meet the rule.

reading.label: Headroom as a multiple of the OBR’s typical forecast error

bands.headline: A normal forecast error would wipe this out.
bands.detail: The OBR’s average absolute error on receipts five years ahead is 0.9% of GDP, about £32bn in 2030-31. Headroom smaller than half that is inside the noise: it tells you little about whether the rule will still be met next year.

bands.headline: Your margin is smaller than the OBR’s own typical forecast error.
bands.detail: The OBR’s average absolute five-year error on receipts is 0.9% of GDP. A Budget inside that margin can be blown off course by revisions that have nothing to do with your decisions.

bands.headline: Your margin is larger than the OBR’s typical forecast error.
bands.detail: Headroom bigger than the OBR’s average absolute five-year receipts error of 0.9% of GDP. An ordinary forecast revision would not by itself put you in breach.

reading.label: Investment rule

bands.headline: Net financial liabilities still fall as a share of the economy.
bands.detail: The investment rule is met. It looks at debt measured as public sector net financial liabilities, which counts financial assets the government owns, so buying an asset with borrowed money does not automatically breach it.

bands.headline: Debt no longer falls in the target year. The investment rule is missed.
bands.detail: The rule requires net financial liabilities to be falling as a share of the economy by the target year. Capital spending does not count against the stability rule, but it does count here.

reading.label: Welfare cap

bands.headline: Capped welfare spending is inside the cap.
bands.detail: The cap is £194.5bn in 2029-30. The state pension sits outside it, so pension decisions do not move this test.

bands.headline: Capped welfare is above the cap but inside the 5% margin.
bands.detail: Where the March forecast left it: £199.2bn against a £194.5bn cap, inside the £204.2bn ceiling. Formally this is a breach of the cap, not of the margin, and the OBR assesses it once a year.

bands.headline: Capped welfare has broken through the margin as well as the cap.
bands.detail: Above the £204.2bn ceiling. The Chancellor must explain the breach to Parliament and set out what will be done about it.

reading.label: Change in borrowing in the target year

bands.headline: You are issuing far less debt than the forecast assumed.
bands.detail: Gilt sales fall with borrowing. What commentators watch after a Budget is the change in the financing remit, not the level of debt: less issuance than expected is the easiest thing for a market to absorb.

bands.headline: Borrowing is a little lower than the forecast assumed.
bands.detail: A modest reduction in gilt issuance. Gilt yields were 5.35% when this Budget was put together against the 4.5% the March forecast assumed, so the direction helps.

bands.headline: Borrowing is roughly where the forecast had it.
bands.detail: Nothing here changes the financing remit much. Gilt yields at 5.35% were already well above the 4.5% the March forecast assumed, which is a bigger fact than anything in this Budget.

bands.headline: You are borrowing more than the forecast assumed.
bands.detail: More gilts to sell into a market where ten-year yields were already 5.35% against the OBR’s 4.5% assumption. The OBR puts the cost of a one percentage point rise in rates at about £15bn a year of borrowing by 2030-31.

bands.headline: A large unfunded increase in borrowing.
bands.detail: An issuance programme well beyond what the forecast assumed, into a market where yields were already 5.35% against the OBR’s 4.5%. The OBR’s own sensitivity says a one percentage point rise in rates costs about £15bn a year by 2030-31, so the reaction can cost more than the measure raised.

reading.label: Change in net financial liabilities in the target year

bands.headline: Debt is on a falling path in the target year.
bands.detail: Net financial liabilities fall as a share of the economy. A falling debt ratio is the thing ratings agencies and gilt investors look at over the medium term, rather than any single year’s deficit.

bands.headline: Debt is flat as a share of the economy.
bands.detail: Neither falling nor rising to speak of. The March forecast had it falling by about 0.8% of GDP in the target year, equivalent to about £27bn.

bands.headline: Debt is rising as a share of the economy in the target year.
bands.detail: The March forecast had net financial liabilities falling by about 0.8% of GDP, roughly £27bn. Reversing that is the change a gilt market notices, whatever the deficit does.

reading.label: Recommendations from colleagues adopted

bands.headline: You adopted none of your colleagues’ recommendations.
bands.detail: Every one of them has organised support behind it. Refusing all of them is a defensible Budget and an exposed one: each campaign now has a vote to point at.

bands.headline: You took a few of your colleagues’ recommendations.
bands.detail: Enough to show you listened, few enough to keep the arithmetic under control. None of these carried an official costing, so each one you adopted is a number you will have to defend.

bands.headline: You adopted most of what your colleagues asked for.
bands.detail: A politically generous Budget. None of these policies has a certified costing, so the more of them you take, the more of your Budget rests on arithmetic nobody else has checked.

reading.label: Decisions from Budget 2025 and the Spending Review reversed

bands.headline: You left your predecessor’s decisions in place.
bands.detail: Continuity has its own argument: every reversal reopens a fight that Parliament has already had once.

bands.headline: You reversed some of your predecessor’s decisions.
bands.detail: Each reversal is a measure Parliament voted for being undone, and the benches that won those votes are still there.

bands.headline: You have unpicked a large part of the last Budget.
bands.detail: Reversing this much invites the charge that the Government does not know its own mind, and every measure has a constituency that organised for it the first time.

reading.label: Change in the tax take as a share of the economy

bands.headline: You have cut the tax take, which was heading for a historic high.
bands.detail: On the March forecast receipts rise from 34.5% of GDP in 2024-25 to 38.5% by 2030-31, which the OBR calls a historic high. You have moved that down.

bands.headline: The tax take is roughly where the forecast had it.
bands.detail: Still heading for 38.5% of GDP by 2030-31 against 34.5% in 2024-25, which the OBR describes as a historic high. Most of that rise is frozen thresholds, not new taxes.

bands.headline: You have pushed the tax take above a level the OBR already calls a historic high.
bands.detail: The forecast had receipts reaching 38.5% of GDP by 2030-31, up from 34.5% in 2024-25. You are adding to that.

bands.headline: A large rise in the tax take, on top of a record one already in the forecast.
bands.detail: Receipts were already forecast to reach 38.5% of GDP by 2030-31 from 34.5% in 2024-25. A rise of this size on top is felt in pay packets and prices well before the target year.

reading.label: Promises made in Downing Street broken

bands.headline: Every promise the Prime Minister asked you to keep survives.
bands.detail: The manifesto tax lock and the last Budget’s commitments stand. MPs in marginal seats have nothing to explain on the doorstep, which is the outcome they wanted most.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT

bands.headline: A promise made in Downing Street is broken, and the marginal seats know which one.
bands.detail: The manifesto was explicit and the last Budget restated it. The MPs who won narrowly will be asked about this first, and the words are on the record.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT

bands.headline: More than one promise is broken.
bands.detail: Each one was made in writing. The marginal seats now have a list, and so does everyone else.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT

reading.label: Welfare decisions of Budget 2025 reversed

bands.headline: The welfare U-turns of last November stand.
bands.detail: Ending the two-child limit was scored as lifting 450,000 children out of poverty. The left of the party fought for that and for the PIP reversal; leaving them in place costs you nothing here.

bands.headline: You have re-run a welfare cut the party fought to reverse.
bands.detail: Reinstating the two-child limit, proceeding with the PIP changes or narrowing winter fuel payments again is the argument of last year run backwards. The Treasury’s own scorecard describes the two-child limit’s removal as lifting 450,000 children out of poverty.

reading.label: Departmental and welfare budgets cut

bands.headline: No department loses money.
bands.detail: Every settlement from the Spending Review stands or grows. Ministers have nothing to write to you about, which is not the same as having nothing to ask for.

bands.headline: A department or two takes a cut, and their ministers say so.
bands.detail: The Spending Review already has unprotected budgets falling in real terms in the later years; a cut on top is felt in a specific service, and the minister responsible will name it.

bands.headline: Cuts across Whitehall: the letters are already being drafted.
bands.detail: Several settlements are below the Spending Review. The OBR notes the squeeze on unprotected departments after 2028-29 is already severe; ministers will argue each one in public.

reading.label: Priorities agreed with the Prime Minister still unfunded

bands.headline: Downing Street got what it agreed.
bands.detail: Every priority from the conversation in Downing Street is funded. The Prime Minister’s programme is in the Budget, which is what the meeting was for.

bands.headline: One priority agreed in Downing Street is not funded.
bands.detail: The Prime Minister set out the programme in public in July and September. A missing piece will be noticed by the people it was promised to.

bands.headline: The Prime Minister’s priorities are not in the Budget.
bands.detail: The programme was set out in public; the Budget does not fund it. Downing Street will read that before anyone else does.

reading.label: Rebellion risk: promises broken, priorities unfunded, welfare reversed, capital spent

bands.headline: The whips expect a quiet vote.
bands.detail: Nothing here breaks a written commitment or reverses what the party fought for. The Budget resolutions pass on the usual numbers.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT

bands.headline: Grumbling, not rebellion.
bands.detail: A concession or an unfunded promise gives the backbenches something to say. The whips can count the votes.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT

bands.headline: The backbenches are restive.
bands.detail: Several things at once: a broken commitment, a missing priority or a welfare reversal. Each has organised support behind it and the whips are counting.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT

bands.headline: An open revolt on the Budget resolutions.
bands.detail: Promises broken and priorities dropped in the same Budget. The people who campaigned on the manifesto now have several reasons to vote against it.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT

reading.label: Headroom against the target you set

bands.headline: Headroom is well below the margin you set out to keep.
bands.detail: The last Budget made a virtue of more than doubling headroom to £21.7bn; commentators had already called the margin wafer-thin before that evaporated. The Bank found gilt moves this year amplified by hedge fund deleveraging. A thin margin is noticed.

bands.headline: Below the target you set yourself.
bands.detail: The margin is smaller than you planned for. The OBR’s typical five-year error is about £32bn, so the difference is one of degree, and the market prices degrees.

bands.headline: Inside your target, narrowly.
bands.detail: You kept the margin you said you would keep. Whether it is enough is the OBR’s forecast error against your headroom, and that comparison is printed on the scorecard.

bands.headline: Comfortably inside the margin you set.
bands.detail: More room than you planned to keep, in a market where thin margins have been punished. The Chancellor’s letter to the Treasury Committee promised a buffer; this is one.

reading.label: Share of the package’s improvement resting on uncertified costings

bands.headline: The package rests on certified costings.
bands.detail: What improves the current budget comes from HMRC rows and Treasury scorecard lines. The OBR will certify those without argument.

bands.headline: A meaningful share rests on figures nobody certified.
bands.detail: Part of the yield comes from measures whose own cards call the figure contested or static. HMRC says a relief’s cost is not the yield from removing it; the OBR scores accordingly.

bands.headline: Most of the yield rests on figures nobody certified.
bands.detail: The package leans on contested bases and static relief costs. The OBR’s re-scoring is where that lands, and the market has read the OBR before.

reading.label: Measures that raise prices

bands.headline: Nothing here pushes prices up.
bands.detail: No VAT, duty or fuel rise. RPI follows the forecast, and index-linked gilts with it.

bands.headline: Price-raising measures feed RPI, and RPI feeds the debt interest bill.
bands.detail: VAT and duty rises pass into prices. The OBR’s sensitivity puts a point on RPI at about £11bn of borrowing by 2030-31, largely through index-linked gilts.

bands.headline: Several price-raising measures at once.
bands.detail: RPI, the index the gilt market watches, will carry the VAT and duty changes into the interest bill. The OBR’s own sensitivity says what a point costs.

reading.label: Breach acknowledged

bands.headline: You are proceeding on your own rules.
bands.detail: No rule is knowingly missed. The Charter’s escape clause stays unused.

bands.headline: You have said openly that a rule will be missed.
bands.detail: The Charter allows suspension in an emergency or a significant shock judged by the OBR; a choice is neither. The Bank’s account of 2025 attributes higher long rates partly to concerns around fiscal sustainability.

reading.label: What the rabbit costs in the target year

bands.headline: A big giveaway in the last minute of the speech.
bands.detail: The rabbit is the headline and its cost is the small print. The last Budget made headroom the headline instead; this one buys applause with it.

bands.headline: A modest surprise for the speech.
bands.detail: Something to cheer that costs less than the room you had. The morning papers will still price it.

bands.headline: No rabbit.
bands.detail: The headroom is the announcement. Fewer cheers in the chamber; fewer questions the next morning.

reading.label: Promised spending scaled back since the desk

bands.headline: Nothing promised was scaled back.
bands.detail: The package that left the desk is the package in the box.

bands.headline: Something promised was scaled back between the desk and the box.
bands.detail: Delays and narrowings are visible to the people who were promised the thing. The Prime Minister set the programme out in public.

bands.headline: Big promises shrank between the desk and the box.
bands.detail: What the Prime Minister announced in July and September is not what the Budget funds. The gap is the story.

reading.label: Threshold freeze kept

bands.headline: The papers notice the tax cut you did not announce: thresholds rise from 2028.
bands.detail: Ending the freeze early lets thresholds rise with prices from April 2028. Frozen thresholds were the largest revenue-raiser in the last Budget, and your predecessor conceded they affect working people.

bands.headline: The morning papers have done the sums on frozen thresholds.
bands.detail: Thresholds stay frozen to April 2031. The OBR says the freeze pulls people into higher bands as earnings grow; the last Chancellor said it would affect working people. That is the tax rise in this Budget that nobody voted on.

reading.label: Share of the package’s improvement resting on uncertified costings

bands.headline: The costings survive a second reading.
bands.detail: Analysts find HMRC rows and Treasury lines behind the yield. Nothing to re-score.

bands.headline: Analysts question the contested costings.
bands.detail: The morning notes go through the measures whose own cards call the base contested. HMRC’s caveat that a relief’s cost is not its yield is quoted back at you.

bands.headline: The yield is doubted in print.
bands.detail: Most of the improvement rests on figures the OBR did not certify as scored. Commentators price the difference.

reading.label: Efficiency savings still pencilled in

bands.headline: You dropped the pencilled-in efficiencies and said so.
bands.detail: The committee notes the honesty: the OBR listed those savings not being realised among the significant risks to departmental spending.

bands.headline: £14bn of efficiencies are still pencilled in, and the committee asks where they are.
bands.detail: The settlements assume technical efficiencies from the Spending Review and more from Budget 2025 by 2028-29. The OBR lists them not being realised as expected among the significant risks. The question is who delivers them.

reading.label: Extra borrowing over the forecast

bands.headline: The gilt remit shrinks.
bands.detail: Less to issue over the forecast than the market expected. The Bank notes sovereign issuance at historically high levels; less of it is welcome.

bands.headline: The financing remit is about what the market expected.
bands.detail: Nothing here changes what the Debt Management Office has to sell.

bands.headline: More gilts to sell over the forecast.
bands.detail: The extra borrowing has to be financed. The Bank notes issuance already at historically high levels and shifting to shorter maturities; the remit grows.

bands.headline: A much larger gilt programme.
bands.detail: The extra issuance over the forecast is large against a market the Bank describes as sensitive to changes in expectations about debt sustainability.

reading.label: Measures that start later than planned

bands.headline: Everything starts when it was promised.
bands.detail: No measure was pushed back to a later year.

bands.headline: The start dates are the story.
bands.detail: One or more measures begin a year or more later than the programme implied. The OBR scores what falls inside the forecast; the department waits.

reading.label: Priorities funded

bands.headline: Nothing new to deliver, so nothing to fall short on.
bands.detail: No funded flagship, so the morning after has no delivery question to ask.

bands.headline: Money is not delivery.
bands.detail: Each funded flagship arrives with the constraints its own documents state: places take years, capacity is not cash, deficits close slower than money moves. The morning papers ask about the second year.

reading.label: Breach acknowledged

bands.headline: No rule is knowingly missed.
bands.detail: The OBR’s assessment on Budget day and yours agree.

bands.headline: The OBR will publish that a rule is missed, and you said so first.
bands.detail: Saying it first is the honest course and it does not change the arithmetic. The escape clause is for a shock the OBR agrees is one.
